newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia's Howard says Australians not racist.
newsitem.headline: Australia's Howard says Australians not racist.

text.p: Australian Prime Minister John Howard on Thursday defended Australians as a tolerant people, but said concerns about high unemployment were fuelling the heated debate on immigration which was engulfing the country.
"I do not believe Australia is made up of a mob of bigots," Howard said in a lengthy Sydney radio interview.

"Australians are to be congratulated, not denigrated, for the extraordinary tolerance and decency (they) have demonstrated over the years to successive waves of migration from different parts of the world," Howard said.
Howard said Australia had the second highest population growth in the developing world in the 1980s, fuelled almost entirely by immigration.

"Because we have high unemployment and because we have gone through a long period of adjustment, economically and socially, there is a great deal of insecurity in the community," Howard said. "It is only natural when you have insecurity that people look around for explanations."
A national debate on immigration and racism was sparked last month when an independent politican made a maiden parliamentary speech claiming the country was being swamped by Asians.
More than seven out of 10 Australian voters now believe immigration levels are too high despite a government plan for further cuts, according to a recent newspaper poll.
"It is inaccurate to say we are being swamped by Asians," said Howard, adding that only 4.8 percent of the population was of Asian background.
Howard said Australia needed an immigration debate, but that it must be a sensitive and tolerant debate.
"The immigration policy is meant to serve the interest of Australia and not to serve the interest of a particular ideology," he said.
"I think the majority of Australians would believe that any reversion to a White Australia policy would be against the interest of this country."
The "White Australia" immigration policy, which ended in the early 1970s, discriminated against non-Anglo Celtic migrants.
"We will never go back in this country to having a discriminatory immigration policy based on race," Howard said.
"I think it is morally, politically and economically in the interest of this country that it is gone."
